newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian minister says Enel now to take LNG.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian minister says Enel now to take LNG.

text.p: Nigerian oil minister Dan Etete said on Thursday that Italian state utility firm Enel would now take the full volume of liquefied natural gas (LNG) it originally signed to buy from Nigeria.

Enel last December cancelled a long-term contract to buy the Nigerian LNG, citing its abandonment of a project to construct a gas plant at Montalto di Castro, north of Rome, for economic, technical and environmental reasons.

"Enel is now taking the entire volume of gas it signed with Nigerian LNG," Etete told reporters at Lagos airport on arrival from an official visit to Italy where he said he had discussed the Enel-Nigeria face-off over the cancellation.
"All issues have been resolved and the Italian government is fully in support of the Nigerian LNG project," he added.
Asked how Enel had solved the problem of its receiving terminal for the Nigerian gas, Etete said that was the Italian company's internal problem.
"What we are concerned with is that they are now taking the gas. How they are going to take it is their problem," he said.
Nigeria immediately launched arbitration in December in Switzerland over the cancellation with its officials saying they were certain to win and recover billions of dollars from Enel.
Enel signed the contract in November and were to receive the first cargo of Nigerian LNG in the third quarter of 1999.

Nigeria's $4 billion LNG project, now in full swing in the southeastern oil-producing area of Bonny, is to produce 7.2 billion cubic metres of LNG per year from a plant projected to start production in 1999.
Enel is to take 3.5 billion cubic metres of the output annually.
Partners in the project are the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation, Shell Gas BV, Elf Aquitaine and Italy's Agip SpA.
Etete debunked some local newspaper reports that Nigeria's government wanted to take controlling shares in the project.
"There is no such thing. It is only speculation," he said.
Long-term supply contracts have been signed with Enargas of Spain, Gaz de France and Botas of Turkey.
